sentences.text: The type specimen of this pterosaur, catalogued as FSAC-OB 232, preserves parts of the skull and lower jaw along with several limb bones including a femur, radius, ulna, humerus, and a fused shoulder blade structure.
Four other fossils attributed to this animal consist entirely of humeri.
The name combines a reference to the Barbary Coast of North Africa with the Greek word for 'finger'.
It possessed upward-curving jaws, a trait shared with other nyctosaurids, a family of pterosaurs.
The fused scapulocoracoid suggests that the animal was likely an adult.
Its long, thin humeral shaft and hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest resemble those of Nyctosaurus more than the pterosaur Alcione.
The ulna is relatively gracile with weakly expanded ends, contrasting with the robust ulna of Alcione.
The femur expands gently rather than showing the strong distal expansion seen in other nyctosaurids, resembling the femur of Pteranodon.
All known specimens were found during a three-year excavation that recovered approximately 200 pterosaur fossils.
Only one fossil occurrence of Barbaridactylus has been recorded.
Barbaridactylus was first described in 2018 by Nicholas R. Longrich, David M. Martill, and Brian Andres.
The genus was named by Longrich and colleagues in 2018.
The ecosystem where it lived included sharks, bony fish, turtles, plesiosaurs, and mosasaurs.
Recent studies indicate that at least five other pterosaur species, including Alcione, Simurghia, and Tethydraco, lived alongside Barbaridactylus at this location.
Barbaridactylus belongs to the family Nyctosauridae.
It is classified as a reptile.
The type species of the genus is Barbaridactylus grandis.
Barbaridactylus lived in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Morocco during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Fossils were found in upper Maastrichtian phosphates in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Northern Morocco.
The layer containing the fossils dates to the latest Maastrichtian, approximately 1 million years before the end-Cretaceous extinction event.
It lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Phylogenetic analysis originally placed Barbaridactylus as the sister taxon of Nyctosaurus lamegoi within the family Nyctosauridae.
Brian Andres suggested in 2022 that Barbaridactylus might actually be an additional species of Nyctosaurus.
A 2024 analysis recovered Barbaridactylus outside the genus Nyctosaurus as the sister taxon of Muzquiopteryx, while reclassifying Nyctosaurus lamegoi as a species of Simurghia.
